explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Paul says, "…I opposed him to his face, because he stood condemned." (Galatians 2:11) To his face means Paul took it up with Cephas directly. I once avoided a hard talk for a whole week, and my mustache got tired just from the dodging.

Paul does write letters, and you're reading one right now. But this time the text says he opposed Cephas "…to his face…" (Galatians 2:11) Nothing here says he wrote Cephas a sharp letter. This was a face-to-face moment, and I bet it got quiet fast.

James comes into the story, but only because certain men come from him (Galatians 2:12). The text never says Paul reports anyone to him. Paul deals with Cephas himself, and the verse says he "…opposed him to his face…" (Galatians 2:11) No paperwork needed.

Yes, baker. Verse 12 says that before certain men came from James, Cephas "…used to eat with the Gentiles." Gentiles are people who aren't Jews. A shared table says a lot, and Cephas was sitting right at it.

Close to the neighborhood, but no. The Pharisees aren't mentioned anywhere in these verses. The verse says Cephas "…used to eat with the Gentiles." (Galatians 2:12) That's the habit Paul is pointing at.

Priests don't show up anywhere in this passage. The verse says that before the men from James arrived, Cephas "…used to eat with the Gentiles." (Galatians 2:12) It's an easy one to guess, and I've guessed worse. I once thought a cookie sheet was a serving tray.

explanations.answer: He's afraid of the circumcision group
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. The text says he drew back and separated himself "…for fear of those in the circumcision group." (Galatians 2:12) Fear changed where he sat. I think we've all picked a seat because of who was watching.

Nope, anger isn't in the verse. The text says Cephas pulled back "…for fear of those in the circumcision group." (Galatians 2:12) So the reason the text gives is fear. I think he was more worried about the room than mad at anybody, and I've dodged a table or two myself.

explanations.answer: He's been called back to Jerusalem
explanations.explanation: The text never says Cephas was called anywhere. It gives a reason, and the reason is fear: he drew back "…for fear of those in the circumcision group." (Galatians 2:12) I think this was one nervous moment at a table, and we've all had those.
That's the word, baker. Paul says, "The other Jews joined him in his hypocrisy…" (Galatians 2:13) He doesn't soften it. Sometimes a hard word is the kind thing to say out loud.
Humility is a good word, but it's not Paul's. He says, "The other Jews joined him in his hypocrisy…" (Galatians 2:13) Pulling away from the Gentiles wasn't humble. Paul calls it hypocrisy.
Paul doesn't call it wisdom at all. Verse 13 says the other Jews "…joined him in his hypocrisy…" That's a heavy word, and he means it. Wisdom would have kept the seat at the table.

True, baker. The text says that "…by their hypocrisy even Barnabas was led astray." (Galatians 2:13) Barnabas had gone up to Jerusalem with Paul (Galatians 2:1), so I think that one stings. It shows how strong the pull of a crowd can be.

It's true, baker. Paul writes, "…by their hypocrisy even Barnabas was led astray." (Galatians 2:13) That word "even" is doing a lot of work. Barnabas had gone to Jerusalem with Paul (Galatians 2:1), and still he got led astray.
Not quite, baker. Paul says, "…I said to Cephas in front of them all…" (Galatians 2:14) So it wasn't private. Everybody could hear it, and I think that made it sting more.
Right, baker. Paul says he spoke to Cephas "…in front of them all…" (Galatians 2:14) Nobody got pulled aside. I think it was a very quiet room for a very loud sentence.

explanations.answer: He pressures Gentiles to live like Jews
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Paul asks, "…how can you compel the Gentiles to live like Jews?" (Galatians 2:14) Cephas was living like a Gentile himself, so the pressure didn't match his own life. Paul points at that gap.

explanations.answer: He hides the gospel from the Jews
explanations.explanation: Paul never says that. His question is, "…how can you compel the Gentiles to live like Jews?" (Galatians 2:14) The trouble is pressure on the Gentiles, not hiding anything from the Jews. Hide the gospel? Friend, Paul says this one out loud in front of them all.

explanations.answer: He ignores the leaders in Jerusalem
explanations.explanation: Nice try, baker, but Paul never says that. His question is about the Gentiles: "…how can you compel the Gentiles to live like Jews?" (Galatians 2:14) Jerusalem isn't anywhere in it. Looking for it in this verse is like digging through a cookie box for a cookie nobody baked. Nothing in there but crumbs, friend!

That's the heart of it, baker. Paul says "…a man is not justified by works of the law, but by faith in Jesus Christ." (Galatians 2:16) Justified means made right with God. It isn't earned, it's trusted. Write that one on your oven door.

Paul says the opposite. A man is "…not justified by works of the law, but by faith in Jesus Christ." (Galatians 2:16) He even adds that "…by works of the law no one will be justified." Perfect or not, the law isn't the way.
Paul was born a Jew himself, and he still says a man "…is not justified by works of the law, but by faith in Jesus Christ." (Galatians 2:16) Birth doesn't do it. Faith in Christ does.
True, baker. Paul says, "So we, too, have believed in Christ Jesus…" (Galatians 2:16) Paul counts himself in that "we," right alongside the Jews by birth he's speaking about. Nobody gets a side door.

It's true, baker. Paul writes, "So we, too, have believed in Christ Jesus, that we may be justified by faith in Christ and not by works of the law…" (Galatians 2:16) The "we" includes Jews by birth like him.
That's Paul's answer, baker. He asks if Christ is a minister of sin, and he says, "Certainly not!" (Galatians 2:17) He doesn't pause or hedge. Just a flat no.
Paul gives no timeline. His answer to the question is "Certainly not!" (Galatians 2:17) There's no little while and no fine print.
Paul doesn't split it up that way. He asks if Christ is a minister of sin and answers, "Certainly not!" (Galatians 2:17) That's one flat no for everybody.

Yes, baker. Paul says, "If I rebuild what I have already torn down, I prove myself to be a lawbreaker." (Galatians 2:18) Building it back up is the very thing that trips him. Tear it down, then leave it down.
Peacemaker sounds nice, but it's not the word. Paul says rebuilding what he tore down would "…prove myself to be a lawbreaker." (Galatians 2:18) Going backward is the trouble.

Paul doesn't say prophet. The verse says, "If I rebuild what I have already torn down, I prove myself to be a lawbreaker." (Galatians 2:18) I'll admit prophet would be a nicer title. Rebuilding just doesn't get him there.

True, baker. Paul writes, "For through the law I died to the law so that I might live to God." (Galatians 2:19) It sounds upside down, but the goal is clear: living to God. I still had to read it twice.
It's true, baker. Paul says, "For through the law I died to the law so that I might live to God." (Galatians 2:19) Dying to the law is not the end of the sentence. Living to God is.
That's right, baker. Paul says, "I have been crucified with Christ, and I no longer live, but Christ lives in me." (Galatians 2:20) It's about as personal as a sentence gets.
Moses is a big name, but he's not who Paul names here. Paul says, "…I no longer live, but Christ lives in me." (Galatians 2:20) The one living in him is Christ.
Elijah doesn't appear in this passage. Paul says, "…I no longer live, but Christ lives in me." (Galatians 2:20) Great name, and no shame in picking it.

explanations.answer: Loved him and gave Himself up for him
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Paul says he lives by faith in the Son of God, "…who loved me and gave Himself up for me." (Galatians 2:20) Notice the "me." He says it so personally that I always want to read it slowly.

explanations.answer: Rewarded him for keeping the law well
explanations.explanation: That's not in the verse. Paul says the Son of God "…loved me and gave Himself up for me." (Galatians 2:20) Paul has just said no one is justified by works of the law (Galatians 2:16), so a reward for law-keeping isn't his point.

explanations.answer: Sent him to teach the law to the Gentiles
explanations.explanation: Sent him to teach? Friend, the verse says nothing like that. Paul says the Son of God "…loved me and gave Himself up for me." (Galatians 2:20) That's what was done for him, not an assignment. It's like opening a gift and finding a to-do list inside.

Not quite, baker. Paul says, "…if righteousness comes through the law, then Christ died for nothing." (Galatians 2:21) So it's the reverse. If the law could do it, His death would have been for nothing.

That's right, baker. Paul says, "…if righteousness comes through the law, then Christ died for nothing." (Galatians 2:21) He says it right after "I do not set aside the grace of God." That's why he holds onto grace.
